title: Regime-Based World Modeling: A Layered Epistemic Architecture for Complex Systems
description: Introduces Regime-Based World Modeling (RBWM), a meta-epistemic framework that maps scientific claims onto a two-axis coordinate system: the Regime axis (R) for emergent complexity levels and the Epistemic Layer axis (L) for derivation distance from observation. It generalizes the Regime-Gating Principle, asserting that claims are valid only when expressed in driver-near variables for the operative regime, thereby preventing regime leakage and clarifying conflicts between models operating at different epistemic coordinates.

key_results.main_finding: RBWM formalizes a two-axis (R,L) mapping with a regime-gating rule that enforces driver-near variables for validity, exposing regime leakage and reconciling apparent theory conflicts as coordinate mismatches.

kill_criteria: KC1: In preregistered, cross-domain benchmarks (≥3 domains spanning R1–R2), models constrained to driver-near L2 variables do not outperform matched L3-construct baselines in out-of-sample prediction (aggregate effect size ≤ 0 with 95% CI excluding positive improvement), falsifying the practical advantage implied by the Regime-Gating Principle.

KC2: Applying the (R,L) coordinate mapping and regime-gated variable selection to established anomaly sets (e.g., rotation curves in galactic dynamics, macroeconomic regime shifts, neural population responses) fails to reduce phantom anomaly rates by at least 20% versus standard pipelines under identical data and calibration, indicating no mitigation of regime leakage.

KC3: Independent expert annotators (≥5) assigning (R,L) coordinates to a diverse corpus (≥200 claims) achieve inter-annotator agreement below Cohen’s kappa 0.6 for both axes after training, demonstrating that the mapping is not operationalizable or reproducible.

KC4: For a canonical cross-regime conflict (e.g., ΛCDM vs MOND rotation-curve claims), re-expression at matched (R,L) coordinates does not alter comparative conclusions or reduce contradictions in prospective tests, showing the coordinate framework does not improve epistemic comparability.

KC5: Demonstrated counterexample where an L3 theoretical construct produces consistent first-order causal control in a fixed regime while all candidate L2 variables are inert under intervention (no first-order effects), violating the driver-proximity requirement central to RGP.
